Business context

Who it's for,
and why now.

THE PRODUCT

A fundraising platform for dioceses

Atlas by GiveCentral serves Catholic diocesan development offices — teams of 5–50 managing thousands of donors across many parishes and legal entities.

THE USERS & THEIR WORLD

Small teams, high stakes, little software help

Gift officers, finance staff and leadership — mostly non-technical and time-poor, on desktop all day with donor visits in between.

THE BUSINESS PROBLEM

Fragmentation costs money

Disconnected tools mean manual reconciliation, reporting lag and missed asks — directly affecting donor retention and revenue.

THE USER PROBLEM

The next action is always a few tabs away

Staff can't see the whole donor or act in the moment, so stewardship slips through the cracks.

Why now: GiveCentral was consolidating point tools into one platform and adding AI (Guru) — the moment to design the connective tissue, not another silo.  ·  Constraints, risks & dependencies: a real multi-entity legal data model, fund-accounting and receipting rules, PCI-handled payments, mixed technical literacy, and eighteen modules that all had to feel like one product — delivered by a small team.
The problem · what teams told us

The data was everywhere.
The work was manual.

Development teams at Catholic dioceses ran world-class fundraising on a patchwork: a spreadsheet for prospects, one tool for email, another for payments, the CRM for records, and exports to stitch it together.

Everything was recorded somewhere — but nothing was connected. The next right action was always a few tabs away.

Research & discovery

From findings
to design calls.

This was a stakeholder-driven redesign, not a formal research study — and I'm explicit about that. What shaped it: conversations with diocesan development leaders, recurring support themes, and a hands-on audit of the existing GiveCentral workflow and comparable nonprofit CRMs.

Stakeholder interviews

Development directors & finance staff.

Support themes

Where users got stuck, repeatedly.

Workflow audit

The current tool, end to end.

Competitive scan

How peer CRMs frame the same jobs.

Finding → implication

Finding: staff jumped between a donor's profile and their giving history constantly.↓Implication: the full donor — giving, pledges, timeline — belongs on one screen.
Finding: the same reports were re-built and exported to Excel every week.↓Implication: make reporting self-serve and repeatable, with saved views.
Finding: major-gift work lived in a spreadsheet no one else could see.↓Implication: bring the pipeline into the platform, visible to the team.
INSIGHT 01

Context before action

People need the whole picture before the next step — not a wall of metrics.

INSIGHT 02

One language, everywhere

Eighteen modules only feel like one product if they share a system.

INSIGHT 03

Depth on demand

Admin power shouldn't crowd the everyday task.

INSIGHT 04

Trust is the product

Money, compliance and access have to feel safe by design.

Research limitations & assumptions: no large-sample usability study or analytics baseline existed at this stage, so findings lean qualitative and some user needs are informed assumptions to validate later. What changed my approach: I started thinking in “modules” and ended thinking in one donor → gift → ask spine — the connections mattered more than any single screen.
Problem framing & strategy

What to solve,
and what to leave.

I reframed eighteen feature requests into a few jobs the platform has to do well — and was deliberate about scope and sequence.

JTBD 01 — “When I open Atlas, help me see what needs me today.”
JTBD 02 — “When I'm about to reach a donor, give me the whole picture in one place.”
JTBD 03 — “When I run an appeal, let me do it end to end without leaving.”
JTBD 04 — “When leadership asks a question, let me answer it myself.”

How I defined success

Fewer tools to run an appeal · less navigation to reach the next action · reporting without an analyst · one coherent system across all modules.

In scope

  • The nine daily-work modules
  • Role-aware dashboard & Donor 360
  • Grounded AI (Guru) as assist, not autopilot
  • One design system across web & mobile

Deliberately out (for now)

  • Deep events & volunteer management
  • Full marketing automation
  • Raw-SQL reporting for all users
  • Native-mobile parity for every module
Prioritization & trade-off: I sequenced by “daily blast radius” — the surfaces every officer touches every day (dashboard, donors, gifts, reports) first; admin depth (roles, integrations, location portal) kept powerful but one layer back. Core hypothesis: if the donor becomes a single workspace and reporting is self-serve, teams consolidate tools and act sooner.
The design direction

Connect the work.
Keep it calm.

One spine, one visual language, and a clear hierarchy — so a 3,800-donor shop can move fast without feeling the weight of eighteen modules.

Set-up and admin stay powerful — but never in the way of the everyday task.

Information architecture & user flows

Simplify the path
before polishing the pixels.

The core job — turn a prospect into a stewarded gift — used to span six tools. The redesign makes it one continuous flow on one record.

Before · across six tools
Spreadsheet → Email tool → Payment → CRM → Excel → Reconcilecontext lost at every hand-off
After · one spine in Atlas
Pipeline → Donor 360 → Record gift → Receipt → Reportone record, updated as you go

Task flow · record a major gift

01

Find donor

Search, or open from pipeline.

02

Review context

Donor 360 — giving, pledges, ask.

03

Record gift

Adaptive form by gift type.

04

Designate

Fund / appeal / entity → GL.

05

Receipt & log

Auto-receipt, writes to history.

Edge cases & error paths I designed for

Unmatched donor

Gift with no donor on file → create-or-match, never block.

Cross-entity view

Financials outside your entity → a clear locked state, not a blank.

Duplicate tax ID

Flagged with a primary marker before it corrupts reporting.

Failed payment / sync

Explicit error + retry; the record is never half-written.

Exploration · before the final direction

Three ways to
hold it together.

Concept A

Module-first (separate apps)

Each area its own mini-app with its own navigation.
Rejected: powerful but fragmented — the original problem in new clothes.
Concept B

Record-first (everything inside the donor)

The donor profile as the whole application.
Rejected: great for 1:1 work, weak for campaigns, reporting and admin at scale.
Concept C ✓

Spine + surfaces (chosen)

One nav spine and shared kit; the donor is a workspace, not the whole app.
Chosen: connects the work and still scales to eighteen modules.
Why C won

It fit the real org model

A diocese is a federation of entities running many campaigns — the platform had to mirror that, not force it into a single record or a pile of apps.
Final UI · the platform, module by module

Nine surfaces,
one experience.

01 · Dashboard

The day,
at a glance.

A role-aware home that leads with what needs a person today — tasks due, pledges to chase, gifts landing — with Guru AI surfacing the three things worth knowing.

What needs me today

Tasks, overdue items and pledges up top — not vanity metrics.

Live KPIs

Gifts today, pledges due, retention, pipeline value at a glance.

Guru AI insights

Grounded, explainable prompts — each with a “why”.

Decision: the dashboard adapts to role (officer vs. finance vs. leadership) rather than showing everyone everything.
02 · Donors

Every donor,
one source of truth.

A fast, filterable list of 3,800+ constituents that opens into Donor 360 — giving, pledges, timeline, relationships and the next action, all on one screen.

Search & segment first

Type, capacity, lifecycle and tags as one-tap filters.

Donor 360

Lifetime, this year, open pledges and last gift — side by side.

Act without leaving

Call, log, task or schedule from the profile.

Decision: the profile is a workspace, not a record — context and the next step live together.
03 · Gifts & pledges

Record any gift
in seconds.

One entry flow handles every gift type — cash, check, card, stock, DAF, IRA, pledges and batches — with matching-gift and receipting built in.

Every gift type, one flow

The form adapts to the type instead of forking into separate tools.

Smart assists

Matching-gift eligibility and card-on-file surfaced inline.

Batch when it counts

Mail-day and pledge batches with an accuracy engine.

Decision: one adaptive form over many type-specific screens — fewer things to learn, fewer places to err.
04 · Campaigns

Run the appeal,
end to end.

Campaigns, funds and appeals in one place — progress to goal, campaign health, and the designations behind every dollar for clean fund accounting.

Progress to goal

Every active campaign, raised vs. target, at a glance.

Funds & appeals, decoupled

Designations map to GL, entity and restriction.

Health, not just totals

Pace, donors and gaps flagged before the deadline.

Decision: separated “campaign” from “fund/appeal” so money can be reported the way finance actually needs it.
05 · Prospect pipeline

Move the major
gift forward.

A shared kanban from identification to stewardship — weighted pipeline, next actions, and Guru AI propensity flags, finally out of the spreadsheet and visible to the team.

Stages that mean something

Identification → qualification → cultivation → solicitation → stewardship.

Weighted forecast

Expected-to-close with a confidence band.

AI ask-timing

Propensity and best-window prompts on each card.

Decision: the pipeline is a team surface — every officer's work is visible, so leadership can coach, not chase.
06 · Reports

Answers without
an analyst.

Pre-built reports, a no-code builder, and saved views — with a shareable report page that replaces the weekly export-to-Excel ritual.

Start from a template

LYBUNT, gifts-by-fund, pledge balance, receipts — ready to run.

Build & save

Filter, group, visualize, and keep it under “Saved by me”.

Schedule & share

Queue a run, export CSV/PDF, or send on a cadence.

Decision: every answer is a reusable, shareable view — not a one-off export that goes stale.
07 · Communications

Reach donors,
track every touch.

Email, appeals and logged activity in one timeline — so the next officer always knows what was said, sent and opened.

One outreach surface

Compose, schedule, and track sends and opens.

Every touch logged

Calls, visits and emails roll into the donor's history.

Performance at a glance

Delivered, opens and status, per message.

Decision: communications write back to the donor record automatically — logging is a by-product, not a chore.
08 · Tasks & reminders

Nothing falls
through.

A shared task list tied to donors and gifts — overdue work, stewardship follow-ups and pledge chases, with saved views and priorities.

Tied to the work

Every task links to a donor, gift or campaign.

Priority & saved views

Overdue, this week, by officer — one click.

At-risk, surfaced

Dollars tied to overdue follow-ups made visible.

Decision: tasks carry their money context — “$84k at risk” beats “3 tasks overdue”.
09 · Users & roles

Enterprise access,
made simple.

Granular, module-level permissions scoped to legal entities — with a visual role builder so admins grant exactly the right access without a spreadsheet of rules.

Roles people understand

Templates per job, then tune per capability.

Scoped to entities

Access follows the diocese's real legal structure.

Readable permission matrix

View / edit / full, module by module.

Decision: a permission summary in plain language — admins see what a role can do before they save it.

Every state, designed

Empty

First-run guidance, not a blank table.

Loading

Skeletons that match the final layout.

Error

Plain-language cause + a way forward.

Success

Confirmation that writes back to the record.

Gated

Entity-locked content shown, not hidden.

The backbone

One system
behind eighteen modules.

None of this scales without a system. Constellation is a three-tier token foundation (primitive → semantic → component) and a reusable kit, so every module is assembled from one language and a change at the token layer updates the whole platform.

Covered in depth in the Constellation design-system case study — foundations, components, states and theming.
1 language
tokens · components · patterns — shared across web & mobile.
The calls that held it together

Cross-cutting
decisions.

Consistency

One IA for eighteen modules

Problem: every module risked its own navigation and patterns.
Decision: a single nav spine + shared component kit.
Trade-off: less per-module freedom — paid back in learnability.
Focus

Role-aware dashboard

Problem: one dashboard can't serve officer, finance and leadership.
Decision: the home adapts its cards to the signed-in role.
Trade-off: more states to design — the right call for relevance.
Trust

Grounded, explainable AI

Problem: AI insight is useless if staff can't trust it.
Decision: Guru is grounded in their data, shows a “why”, never moves money alone.
Trade-off: AI does less autonomously — exactly right for money.
Safety

Entity-gated data

Problem: one donor gives across many legal entities.
Decision: global identity, but financials gated to the viewer's entity.
Trade-off: a visible “locked” state over a confusing blank.
Accessibility

Considered,
not claimed.

Contrast-aware semantic tokens, keyboard navigation with visible focus, explicit empty / loading / error states, clear form labels, and adequate targets. Designed for — not formally audited to — WCAG.

Validation & iteration

Tested the thinking,
then tightened it.

Validation at this stage was design reviews and clickable-prototype walkthroughs with stakeholders — not a formal, sampled usability study. I'm clear about that, and about what it did and didn't tell me.

What I was checking

Can someone find a donor and record a gift without help? Can they build a report without exporting? Is “what needs me today” really the right first screen?

First pass
Reports opened into a builder

Reporting dropped users straight into a blank query builder — reviewers froze.

Revised
Templates first, builder second

Pre-built reports up front, the builder one click deeper, every result saveable & shareable.

First pass
A dashboard full of metrics

A wall of KPIs answered “how are we doing”, not “who's next”.

Revised
Action before analytics

Tasks, pledges due and at-risk dollars lead; metrics sit below.

Remaining concerns to test with real users: whether role-based dashboards match how teams actually split work, whether the single gift-entry form stays simple across every type, and whether “gated vs. hidden” financials read clearly the first time.
Outcomes & business impact

What changed.

  • Six disconnected tools consolidated into one connected platform
  • A multi-screen donor lookup collapsed into a single Donor 360 workspace
  • Weekly “export to Excel” replaced by self-serve, shareable reports
  • Major-gift pipeline moved out of a private spreadsheet and onto a team surface
  • A reusable design system (Constellation) spanning eighteen modules
Projected
↓ time
Faster donor lookup
One workspace vs. hunting across screens.
Projected
↑ rate
More self-serve reporting
Saved views vs. manual exports.
Projected
↓ tools
Fewer systems to run an appeal
Six tools → one platform.
An honest note: Atlas is a prototype, so the arrows above are expected directions, not measured results. The first step after launch is to instrument lookup time, report self-serve rate and tool consolidation — and let real numbers replace them.
“This is the first time the whole donor — giving, pledges and the next ask — is on one screen. That alone changes how an officer preps a visit.”— paraphrased from stakeholder review feedback
Measured vs. unmeasured: the structural outcomes above are real and verifiable in the product (tool count, screens-per-task, module coverage, one design system). Behavioural outcomes — time saved, adoption, conversion, retention — are not yet measured; instrumenting them is the first post-launch step. No numbers here are invented.
Collaboration & delivery

From design
into a real product.

With Product
Framed the jobs & scope together; sequenced what shipped first by daily blast radius.
With Engineering
Checked feasibility early and mapped every design token 1:1 to CSS variables for a clean handoff.
With Finance & stakeholders
Pressure-tested fund-accounting, receipting and the multi-entity model against real rules.
Handling disagreement
Wrote decisions as problem → decision → trade-off, so debates were about evidence, not taste.
Handoff & consistency: components shipped with their states (empty, loading, error, gated) and specs, all built from one Constellation kit so modules stay consistent as they're built. Constraints & compromises I designed around: PCI-handled payments, a real legal-entity hierarchy, and a small team — which pushed me toward reuse over bespoke screens, and toward AI that assists rather than acts. QA: I reviewed built screens against the specs and states, and fed fixes back before sign-off.

Reflection

What I learned.

The hard part of a platform isn't drawing eighteen screens — it's deciding what each person needs at each moment, so power never turns into clutter. The design system was what let one person keep that many surfaces coherent.

What I'd do differently: bring engineering into the IA exploration even earlier, especially around the multi-entity data model, before committing to a direction.

WHAT WORKED

The system paid for itself

Building Constellation first made every later module faster and more consistent — one person could keep eighteen surfaces coherent.

WHAT I'D CHANGE

Engineer the data model sooner

The multi-entity, entity-gated model touched everything; it deserved engineering input before the IA locked.

UNEXPECTED

Trust was the real feature

For money and AI, legibility — “why am I seeing this?” — mattered more than cleverness.

WHAT I LEARNED

Connections > screens

The value wasn't any one module — it was the donor → gift → ask spine that joined them, and that's what I'd investigate and measure next.
